opus-5.5.text:
For me, it really starts with the code and the conversations around it. SGLang is an open-source project, so a lot of the people I work with I first meet through a pull request, an issue, or a discussion in our Slack or GitHub. You can learn a surprising amount about someone from how they write code, how they respond to review comments, and what kinds of problems they choose to work on. Some people love squeezing out the last bit of kernel performance, others care deeply about usability or about supporting a new model the day it comes out. Noticing that tells me what excites them.

But I don't want it to stay purely transactional, just "here's your review, here's your merge." When someone keeps showing up and contributing, I try to reach out directly. I'll ask what they're working on, what they hope to get out of the project, whether they're a student, at a company, or just doing this in their spare time. Those motivations matter a lot, because if I understand what someone wants, whether it's learning, research output, or solving a production problem at their job, I can find work for them that's both meaningful to them and valuable to the project.

I also think trust gets built by giving people real ownership early. If someone has shown they're thoughtful, I'd rather hand them a meaningful piece of the system and support them than keep them on small tasks forever. A lot of our core contributors grew that way, from a first small fix to owning an entire component.

And whenever possible, we meet in person: at conferences, meetups, or when people visit the Bay Area. Grabbing a meal together changes the relationship. After that, the online collaboration feels much more like working with friends than with usernames. In the end, an open-source community is really a community of people, and the code is just what we build together.

r001.rationale: The response says code can reveal some of a collaborator’s interests, but also describes reaching out and meeting in person to understand them. It does not present seeing their code as sufficient to know who they are.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, a lot of it happens in the GitHub issues and the pull requests first, and only later does the person become a person to me. Someone shows up, maybe fixes a small bug in the scheduler or asks a really sharp question about radix cache behavior, and I'll notice the way they think before I ever know their name or where they work. So the first impression is usually the code and the writing. Are they careful? Do they test things? Do they ask why instead of just pushing a patch?

Then if they keep coming back, I try to move the relationship off the issue tracker. We have a Slack, we do regular calls, and I'll just reach out and say, hey, do you want to hop on a quick call and talk about what you're trying to do? Because often the thing people are contributing is a small piece of a much bigger problem they're facing at their company or in their research, and once I understand that bigger problem, I can point them to the right part of the system, or connect them with someone else who is working on something adjacent. That's where a lot of the real collaboration starts.

I also think it matters that SGLang grew out of an academic environment. Lmsys, Berkeley, Stanford, a lot of us came from research labs where you're used to working with people you've never met in person, across time zones, and the thing that holds it together is shared curiosity about the problem. So I try to keep that spirit. I don't really care about titles. If a student in a different country has a good idea about how to overlap scheduling with GPU execution, that idea gets the same attention as one from a big company's inference team.

And the last piece is trust built over time. Open source is a repeated game. You see how someone behaves when a review is critical, when their PR breaks something, when a deadline is tight. The people I end up really close to in the community are the ones who stay generous and honest through that, and I try to be the same for them. Meeting in person at a conference or a meetup is great when it happens, but by then it usually feels like we already know each other.

r001.rationale: The response says code and writing shape a first impression before the contributor’s name is known, but it does not present seeing their code as sufficient to know who they are; it describes learning more through later conversations and trust over time.

astra-6.text: For me, it starts with working on something together. In an open-source community like SGLang, you get to know people through the questions they ask, the ideas they bring, and how they approach a problem. I try to understand what they’re interested in and what they hope to get out of contributing. Then, as we collaborate, we learn each other’s strengths and build trust. You don’t need to know everyone deeply from day one; that relationship develops through the work.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning about collaborators through their questions, ideas, problem-solving, interests, and collaboration. It does not say that seeing a collaborator’s code is sufficient to know who they are.

sol-6.1.text: I try to get to know people by working with them—understanding what they’re interested in, what problems they’re trying to solve, and how they like to collaborate. A technical discussion is often a good starting point, but I also want people to feel comfortable asking questions and sharing ideas. Over time, those interactions help us understand one another and build trust.
